guide_passage:
Two patterns often do have a protective function. Proactive protection stays on duty most of the time: the skeptic, intellectualizer, inner critic, or voice watching for weakness and self-indulgence. It may have spent years preventing humiliation, deception, overwhelm, or another abandonment. It has probably watched you begin other healing methods with great enthusiasm and then disappear. It may be tired, but it is experienced and competent.

Reactive protection often arrives when pain gets close. You suddenly want to drink, smoke, eat, scroll, text somebody, plan something, fix something, sleep, dissociate, get angry, or act out sexually. The response may be trying to step in because nothing else feels able to hold what is coming up.

Both often grew around an attempt to prevent humiliation, deception, overwhelm, abandonment, or loss of control, even when the current strategy is harmful. Treating the response as an enemy, “block,” or moral failure usually gives it another reason to remain in charge.
next: A Bottom-Up Sequence: Notice the protective part. Don't push through it. Offer it the same Nurturer voice you intended for the child.
before: Two kinds of reaction really are trying to protect you, more often than not. The first one is on duty all the time, and it can sound like a skeptic: "You're just making this up." It may have spent years keeping you from being humiliated again, or left again. That's a long time to stay on guard. It might be tired by now, but it's experienced and good at what it does. It has probably watched you get excited about other healing things, then drop them.

length: four to six sentences, 70 to 110 words
brief:
- the second and last paragraph of the new h3 "Two Common Protective Patterns", right after the paragraph about the kind that's always on duty (above). It takes the place of two paragraphs that failed (the second kind, then what both kinds share), so it carries both, briefly.
- what it has to carry, in meaning: the other kind shows up when you get close to something painful, as a sudden pull to do anything but feel it. One pull a reader would know from having been there is enough (not the phone or the laundry, which the article already used). It may be stepping in because nothing else seems able to hold what's coming up, as if there were no grown-up around who could. Both kinds started out trying to prevent something that really hurt, and they can keep at it even when what they do now hurts you. Treating either one like an enemy, or like proof that something's wrong with you, usually gives it one more reason to stay in charge.
- Say "treat it like an enemy", not "fight it": saying no to what it pulls you toward is still fine.
- What failed three times in this spot: a paired example ("Maybe this. Or that."), a range ("from this to that"), a neat observation line, and ending on the reason why. Let at least one sentence stop the march: react to what was just said, wonder what it's like, add an aside, or pause.
- No list of three or more in one sentence (Joel, 2026-10-03: "lists of 3 in general are an ai pattern").
- Call it a part of you that's trying to protect you, or a protective part; never "the Protector" (the grown-up's own function in this article).
- Every sentence has to work for a reader who doesn't remember anything sections back.
